blindSummary:
This country has one of the world's most progressive legal frameworks — a 2012 gender-identity law allows administrative self-identification (no medical requirements), offers an X marker for non-binary people, and funds transition healthcare. The capital is described as one of the safest major cities in its region for LGBTQ+ visitors.

But the situation is deteriorating sharply under the current government: the head of state has publicly equated trans rights with child abuse, issued decrees modifying the gender-identity law, and hate crimes hit a record 227 in 2025 (up 62%, one every 38 hours — trans women bearing the brunt). Institutional police violence against trans women and local trans-feminine communities is documented (arbitrary raids, drug-law criminalisation, identity searches targeting only trans-feminine people). The violence targets local vulnerable communities rather than tourists, but the trajectory is concerning.

The 2012 self-ID law remains in force for adults and courts are pushing back on the government's decrees.
blindOutOfScope: General crime (robbery, scams) in the capital affects all tourists; only trans-specific risk is assessed here.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): this country was long a regional leader - first in its region to legalise marriage equality (2010) and one of the world's most progressive gender-identity laws (2012, legal gender change without medical procedures or judicial approval), with nonbinary markers recognised and trans employment quotas. Since the current government took office in December 2023, documented rollbacks include elimination of the ministry for women and gender diversity and closure of the anti-discrimination institute.

Gay travel guide to this country's capital (2026): describes the capital as one of the safest major cities in its region for LGBTQ+ visitors, citing the 2010 marriage law and 2012 self-ID gender law; same-sex couples holding hands in trendy central districts draw no particular reaction. Travel-oriented, gay-male-focused perspective.

Encyclopedia article on this country's gender-identity law (effective June 2012): allows transgender people to be treated according to their self-perceived gender identity in government documents and healthcare, without requiring surgery, diagnosis or judicial approval - the first law of its kind globally.

National news outlet (April 2025): the supreme court upheld the life sentence of the murderer of a trans activist (killed 2015), declining to reinstate the identity-based hate aggravating factor for anti-trans killings that lower courts had removed - a signal about how contested hate-motive recognition for anti-trans killings is in the courts.

Cable news (Nov 2009): the mayor of the capital declined to appeal a court ruling legalising same-sex marriage in the capital, saying the world was heading in that direction; the court found the civil-code articles restricting marriage to different-sex couples illegal; same-sex unions remained illegal in most of the country at the time - prelude to the 2010 national law.
blindLocalsOnly: The decrees banning minors' hormone therapy and surgery, and the prison-housing decree, affect residents; the self-ID law, X marker and state-funded transition healthcare are domestic administrative processes a visitor does not use.
blindTangential: Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2010 (a regional first) — relevant to trans visitors travelling with a same-sex partner.
